Frederick II of Legnica
fred'rik
n. (1480–1547; Duke of Legnica and Brieg, the first prince to establish the Reformation in Silesia)
Frederick, from Old High German fridu, peace, and rihhi, rule; a name meaning peaceful ruler.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Frederick II was Duke of Legnica from 1488 and of Brieg from 1521, a Piast prince of the old Silesian line. He took up the Reformation early, by 1522 and formally in 1524, and was the first ruler in Silesia to establish it in his duchies — appointing evangelical preachers, ordering visitations, dissolving monasteries, and in 1526 founding at Liegnitz a university on the Wittenberg pattern. That foundation collapsed within three years, partly because the duke had also become Caspar Schwenckfeld's patron and the school took on the spiritualist colouring that followed Schwenckfeld everywhere. Frederick later distanced himself and Schwenckfeld left Silesia for good in 1529. The dictionary records him for the thing he did well and for the model: Jehoshaphat sent teachers through his own towns with the book in their hands. “And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them” (2Ch 17:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a duke as a sovereign prince, the ruler of a duchy; mercy as that benevolence which disposes to overlook injuries; and to uphold as to support, to sustain, to keep from falling.

expand to see more

DUKE, n. [L. dux, a leader.] A sovereign prince, ruler of a state called a duchy; a nobleman of the highest order.

MERCY, n. That benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to treat an offender better than he deserves.

UPHOLD, v.t. To support; to sustain; to keep from falling or declining; to maintain.

VISITATION, n. The official visit of a superior to a church or district for inspection and correction.

STATUTE, n. [L. statutum.] An act of the legislature; a law; a special law or ordinance.

Key Scripture

2Ch 17:9 — "And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people."

2Ch 17:7 — "Also in the third year of his reign he sent to his princes, even to Benhail, and to Obadiah, and to Zechariah, and to Nethaneel, and to Michaiah, to teach in the cities of Judah."

Deu 17:19 — "And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them:"

Pro 20:28 — "Mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy."

Modern Corruption

Duke of Legnica and Brieg, the first Silesian prince to establish the Reformation, who founded a university at Liegnitz in 1526 and was for a time Schwenckfeld's patron.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Frederick's entry has to hold a real failure alongside a real achievement. He was first in Silesia, and first is worth something. He also gave Schwenckfeld a court, a hearing and a university, and Schwenckfeld's doctrine of the celestial flesh of Christ and his disparagement of the sacraments and of the external word spread from Legnica outward and troubled Silesian Lutheranism for a century. A prince who protects a teacher before he has weighed the teaching has used his office to amplify something he does not understand.

The principle to recover is the shape of Jehoshaphat's reform, which is the Bible's own picture of a godly ruler and has two features worth marking. He sent men out rather than summoning people in, and the five princes are named one by one before their errand is stated: “to teach in the cities of Judah” (2Ch 17:7). And what the teachers carried was not the duke's programme but a text: “And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them” (2Ch 17:9). The king himself is to read it all his life (Deu 17:19), and his throne is upheld by mercy rather than by his patronage of clever men (Pro 20:28).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lamad (H3925), to teach; Hebrew chesed (H2617), mercy or steadfast love.

expand to see more

Hebrew lamad (H3925) — to teach, to instruct; 2 Chronicles 17:7 and 17:9.

Hebrew sepher (H5612) — a book, a writing, a scroll; “the book of the law of the LORD”, 2 Chronicles 17:9.

Hebrew qara' (H7121) — to call, to read aloud; “he shall read therein”, Deuteronomy 17:19.

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — mercy, kindness, steadfast love; Proverbs 20:28.

Hebrew sa'ad (H5582) — to support, to uphold, to sustain; Proverbs 20:28.

Usage

"“And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them” (2Ch 17:9) — evangelical preachers appointed and visitations ordered from 1524."

"“to teach in the cities of Judah” (2Ch 17:7) — the Liegnitz university foundation of 1526."

"“and he shall read therein all the days of his life” (Deu 17:19) — the standard by which his patronage of Schwenckfeld is judged."
